# Archetypal Forms {#sec-archetypes}

Certain designs keep turning up. A farmer's flock under panels, a prairie strip in a wet draw, a retired irrigated field: the same few arrangements appear on ground that has nothing else in common. They recur because the pressures on a project are never evenly matched. Cost and financing and energy yield push hardest nearly everywhere, and where nothing pushes back, the result is the same array anywhere in the country. Where something does push back, and keeps pushing through permitting and every round of cost cutting, the design settles into a shape that answers it. An **[archetype](terminology.qmd#term-archetype)** is one of those settled shapes. The names describe patterns found in built projects, given after the fact, and a pattern can disappear when the policy or the market that let a pressure win is taken away. Some rest on many projects and some on one so far, and the Archetype Catalog lists what has been found.

![**How an archetype emerges.** Position along the bottom is one way the nine [design pressures](design-pressures.qmd) can come out; height is the conflict left standing. The low spots that keep collecting projects are archetypes, six of them named here with their codes. The dashed profile is an arid region.](../figures/fig_archetypes_emerge.svg){#fig-archetypes-emerge}

## Thirteen forms at a glance {#sec-scale-position}

Every archetype carries a code that combines three earlier chapters: its zone on the scale transect, its position on the farming axis, and the lever that leads its restorative work. So `A1 scale · S1 farming · ownership-led restoration` is a farmstead array on ground the farm's own animals keep using, made restorative by who owns it.

![**Where the archetypes sit.** Each form is drawn across the zones it recurs at, in the row of its farming-axis position, and colored by the lever that leads its restorative work. Filled bars are the six featured forms, outlined bars the seven sketched ones, and dashed bars a position a form takes only in some cases. Hatched cells are combinations that rarely get built; a clear cell with no bar is possible, with no recurring form yet.](../figures/fig_archetype_map.svg){#fig-archetype-map}

The map carries four readings. The primary-agriculture row runs the whole transect, because keeping a pasture under panels takes nothing but putting the array where the stock already were. The hatching shows where sparing is rare: at the small end, where an acre or two spares almost nothing, and for low-productivity siting at A5, where brightfields alone reach. A clear cell is still possible even without a bar. Created agriculture happens at every size, from a grazed landfill under a utility array to a garden kept with hives inside a small civic one. Ten of the thirteen forms reach A3, more than any other zone. And read from left to right, the colors tend to move from ownership and structure through siting and scale to management and contracts. That is Chapter 5's claim drawn form by form: restoration changes tools as projects grow.

## Six featured archetypes {#sec-featured}

Each featured form is drawn in section at its own scale, with the same three-meter panel in every drawing and the sun from the upper left, so the shade bands fall where the shade actually lands. Its [outcomes footprint](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale) sits beside the drawing. The footprints are judgments about forms, not measurements, and each named project illustrates its form rather than having been audited against it.

### Barnyard Shelter Solar

[A1](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) scale · **[S1](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** farming · *[ownership-led](restorative-work.qmd#sec-leads)* restoration

![Barnyard shelter solar in section. The array is sized to the parlor rather than to the grid, which pushes Agriculture out toward the rim and leaves Ecology short of the ring. The drawing carries what the profile cannot: shade gathers the herd, and the ground beneath it compacts.](../figures/fig_arch_barnyard.svg){#fig-arch-barnyard}

Roughly 10 to 100 kilowatts stand over the yard or paddock the farm's own animals already use, high enough for them to shelter beneath, with the power running behind the meter to the milking parlor and the well pump. The same farmer owns the animals, the array, and the labor, so little has to be written down to line their interests up. The form gives up generating at scale, and the ground pays for the shade: the herd gathers under it, and the soil there compacts. At the University of Minnesota's research dairy in Morris, a 30-kilowatt array shades thirty to forty cows, which ran about a degree cooler. [Full entry →](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-barnyard)

### Perennial Crop Canopy

[A2–A4](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) scale · **[S1](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** farming · *[structure-led](restorative-work.qmd#sec-leads)* restoration

![Perennial crop canopy in section. One panel row rides above each crop row rather than between them, and the planting keeps its trellis and its roots for the whole life of the array. Agriculture reaches nearest the rim, and Ecology sits just inside the ring, because what carries on underneath is intensive horticulture.](../figures/fig_arch_perennial_crop.svg){#fig-arch-perennial-crop}

Panels go over a planting that is not lifted between harvests: vines, tree fruit, trellised canes, or wild blueberry. Over low fruit the array is nearly a conventional one, and over vines and trees it becomes a canopy four or five meters up. The crop's life and the array's are the same length, which is what makes the form structure-led. At the tall end it costs 1.8 to 2.7 times a conventional mount, and cost and financing is the pressure it gives way to. At the low-growing end the geometry barely departs from a conventional array, and at Maces Pond in Maine that shaded a blueberry field out of commercial harvest [@calderwood2025]. Colorado has tall canopies over chardonnay and peaches. [Full entry →](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-permanent-crop)

### Marginal Land Solar

[A2–A3](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) scale · **[S4](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions)**, or **[S1](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** where stock stays on · *[siting-led](restorative-work.qmd#sec-leads)* restoration

![Marginal land solar in section. The siting decision is the archetype: the array takes the wet, stony corner and the field keeps farming. Communities, Water, and Ecology all sit well out toward the rim, and Agriculture is the one pulled back to the ring.](../figures/fig_arch_marginal.svg){#fig-arch-marginal}

The array takes the flood-prone corners, rocky headlands, and wet remnants that no longer pay their way, and leaves the better fields to farm, at 100 kilowatts to 3 megawatts on 1 to 20 acres. Whatever made a parcel poor for farming often makes it poor for solar too, so cost and financing is the pressure it fights. The form exists for income from acres that were not paying. At Cozy Cove Farm in Gurley, Alabama, a 50-kilowatt array stands seven feet over a flood-prone corner of riverside pasture that the herd still grazes, which makes that site the sharing version, at S1. At 50 kilowatts it is also below the form's A2–A3 range, in A1, so the one documented case sits just outside the category it illustrates. [Full entry →](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-marginal)

### Solar Prairie Strips

[A3](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) scale · **[S5](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** farming · *[siting-led](restorative-work.qmd#sec-leads)* restoration

![Solar prairie strips in section. Water reaches almost to the rim and Agriculture falls inside the ring, which is the trade this form makes on purpose. The mechanism is visible: runoff intercepted on the contour, sediment held at the upslope edge, roots well below crop depth.](../figures/fig_arch_prairie_strips.svg){#fig-arch-prairie-strips}

A distribution-scale array of one to five megawatts is paired with deep-rooted prairie planted where the field sheds water: contour bands, low draws, and wet corners. The array, often sold as [community solar](terminology.qmd#term-community-solar), pays for the planting. Placement this precise is a tool for the middle of the transect, and it runs out at a few hundred acres, where the substation and the land market choose the ground. At Ramsey Renewable Station in Minnesota, 3.4 megawatts sit on a native ground layer that, in DOE's modeling, absorbed the 100-year design storm on sandy soil with no detention basins at all. [Full entry →](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-prairie-strips)

### Regenerative Solar Grazing

[A2–A5](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) scale · **[S1–S2](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** farming · *[management-led](restorative-work.qmd#sec-leads)* restoration

![Regenerative solar grazing in section. Water reaches furthest, on held cover and year-round roots, while Communities is pulled just inside the ring, because at the scale drawn the agriculture is a tenancy rather than the farm's own operation. Clearance is the quiet constraint: panels this low settle the question of stock as sheep.](../figures/fig_arch_grazing.svg){#fig-arch-grazing}

A flock moves through a planned rotation under an array of anything from a few acres to several thousand. Clearance and water points decide the stock, which in practice means sheep. In the commercial zone the flock is usually the landowner's own, and from the community zone up it is more often hired in. Two calendars have to fit together, since the power plant wants the grass kept low on its schedule and the shepherd moves the flock on the flock's. Grazing costs about what mowing does [@mccall2023], so a budget built on saving money will come up short. Aurora Solar's 150 megawatts across sixteen Minnesota sites are kept by thousands of contracted sheep. [Full entry →](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-grazing)

### Retired-Irrigation Solar

[A4–A5](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) scale · **[S5](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** farming · *[contract-led](restorative-work.qmd#sec-leads)* restoration

![Retired-irrigation solar in section. Agriculture falls inside the ring by design and Water reaches almost to the rim. The dashed line is the counterfactual, and the claim holds only where governance keeps the saved water from being pumped somewhere else.](../figures/fig_arch_retired_irrigation.svg){#fig-arch-retired-irrigation}

Irrigated fields above an overdrawn aquifer come out of production under a large array, commonly 50 megawatts and up, and the panels need no water. Choosing the ground takes the fields out of farming, but only retiring the water right keeps the water in the aquifer, and a water right lives on paper. That is what makes the form contract-led. Where the metering and the rules are loose, the farming stops and the saving never arrives [@zwickle2021]. Westlands Solar Park in California's San Joaquin Valley is part of a plan to convert up to about 136,000 acres under the state's groundwater law [@stid2022]. [Full entry →](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-water)

::: {.callout-tip .running-example icon=false title="At Rabbit Hills"}
The primer's thread ends in a full description: `A3 scale · S1 farming · management-led restoration`. Each part of that code came from a different chapter. The scale transect placed it in the community zone. The farming axis placed it at S1, because the sheep pasture is still a sheep pasture. And management leads its restorative work: a flock kept on the ground. Among the archetypes it is Regenerative Solar Grazing, with the university's own flock doing the grazing.
:::
